subject: fr
title: Ind AS 103 Business Combinations
summary: Business vs asset · acquirer & reverse acquisition · consideration & contingent consideration · PPA exceptions · goodwill/bargain · measurement period · common control (pooling)
currency: SM May 2026 onwards (Nov 2024 ed., Aug 2025 reprint) · questions swept May 2022 – Nov 2026 RTP/MTP

sections.title: Scope and what is a business

cards.front: Scope and what a business combination is: what is the rule?

back.simplified: A business combination is a transaction or other event in which an acquirer obtains control (as defined in Ind AS 110) of one or more businesses . Two elements: control is obtained, and the acquiree is a business. Ind AS 103 does not apply to (a) the formation of a joint arrangement, (b) the acquisition of an asset or group of assets that is not a business (asset acquisition), and (c) business combinations of entities under common control (dealt with by Appendix C).
back.explanation: Control may be obtained by transferring cash or other assets, incurring liabilities, issuing equity, a mix, or without consideration — by contract alone (then NCI may be 100%). Structures: subsidiaries, legal merger of net assets, transfer to a newly formed entity (roll-up), or former owners of one entity obtaining control of the combined entity.

cards.front: Memory hook: Scope and definition of business combination?

back.simplified: BC = Control + Business.

cards.front: Definition of a business, substantive process and the concentration test: what is the rule?

back.simplified:
A business is an integrated set of activities and assets capable of being conducted and managed to provide goods or services to customers, generate investment income or other income from ordinary activities. Elements: input , process , output . At a minimum it must include an input and a substantive process that together significantly contribute to the ability to create output; outputs are not required.
 Substantive process — without outputs: critical to developing/converting inputs into outputs and an organised workforce plus other inputs it could develop; with outputs: critical to continue producing outputs with an organised workforce, or significantly contributes and is unique/scarce or c
back.explanation: Gross assets for the test exclude cash and cash equivalents, deferred tax assets and goodwill from DTL; include consideration (plus NCI and previously held interest at fair value) in excess of net identifiable assets. Practical computation: consideration incl. NCI and previous interest + liabilities assumed (excl. DTL) − cash/DTA. Land and building attached together = one asset. Not similar: tangible vs intangible, different classes, financial vs non-financial, same class with very different risks.
cases: SM Example 1: 300 + 120 + 80 + 800 − 200 = ₹1,100 crore gross assets; building ₹1,000 crore = 91% → asset acquisition (judgement on 'substantially all').

Investment property with ancillary outsourced services → usually asset acquisition (SM Example 4); multi-tenant property with employees managing leases → business (Example 5). Shell company → not a business, no goodwill (Example 7).

cards.front: Memory hook: Is it a business? Concentration test?

back.simplified: Business = Input + Substantive process (output optional). Concentration test passes → asset purchase.

sections.title: Acquirer, reverse acquisition and acquisition date

cards.front: Step 1 — identifying the acquirer: what is the rule?

back.simplified: The acquirer is the entity that obtains control (Ind AS 110: power, exposure to variable returns, ability to use power to affect returns — considering potential voting rights and substantive rights). If unclear: in a cash/asset/liability deal, usually the entity that pays ; in an equity exchange, usually the entity that issues shares — but consider (a) relative voting rights after the combination, (b) a large minority voting interest, (c) composition of the governing body, (d) senior management, (e) who pays a premium, (f) relative size, and who initiated it.
back.explanation: Company A, much larger, issues 20% of combined capital to B's shareholders → A is acquirer (SM Example 8). Company A issues 70% of combined capital to the larger B's shareholders who take over management → B is the accounting acquirer; A is the legal acquirer (Example 9). A new entity formed to issue shares is not usually the acquirer, but a NewCo paying cash after new investors obtained control of it can be (SM Example 11).
cases: Company A, much larger, issues 20% of combined capital to B's shareholders → A is acquirer (SM Example 8). Company A issues 70% of combined capital to the larger B's shareholders who take over management → B is the accounting acquirer; A is the legal acquirer (Example 9).
A new entity formed to issue shares is not usually the acquirer, but a NewCo paying cash after new investors obtained control of it can be (SM Example 11).

cards.front: Memory hook: Identifying the acquirer?

back.simplified: Acquirer clues: Votes, Minority block, Board, Management, Premium, Size, Initiator.

cards.front: Reverse acquisitions: what is the rule?

back.simplified: A reverse acquisition occurs when the entity that issues securities ( legal acquirer ) is the acquiree for accounting purposes , and the legal acquiree is the accounting acquirer (e.g. a private operating company reverse-merging into a listed shell). The accounting acquiree must be a business. Consideration is measured as the fair value of the number of shares the accounting acquirer would have had to issue to give the legal acquirer's owners the same percentage of the combined entity.
back.explanation: SM Example 9 (reverse acquisition): A issues 2.5 shares per B share (1,50,000 shares); B's owners hold 83.33%. B would have issued 30,000 ÷ 2.5 = 12,000 shares × ₹105 = ₹12,60,000; goodwill = 12,60,000 − 11,00,000 = ₹1,60,000. Consolidated statements are issued in the legal parent's name but are a continuation of the legal subsidiary's (accounting acquirer's) financial statements.
cases: SM Example 9 (reverse acquisition): A issues 2.5 shares per B share (1,50,000 shares); B's owners hold 83.33%. B would have issued 30,000 ÷ 2.5 = 12,000 shares × ₹105 = ₹12,60,000; goodwill = 12,60,000 − 11,00,000 = ₹1,60,000.

cards.front: Memory hook: Reverse acquisition?

back.simplified: Reverse = the paper buyer is the real target.

cards.front: Step 2 — the acquisition date: what is the rule?

back.simplified: The acquisition date is the date the acquirer obtains control — usually the closing date (consideration transferred, assets acquired, liabilities assumed) but it can be earlier or later (e.g. a written agreement giving control before closing). Consider all facts. It fixes when consideration, assets, liabilities and NCI are measured and from when the acquiree is consolidated.
back.explanation: SM Example 12: control of the board obtained on 1 July 20X1 → acquisition date 1 July, not the 1 April 'appointed date', 1 June agreement, 15 July payment or 1 August share transfer. Court-approved schemes and regulatory approvals: control usually does not pass until substantive approvals are obtained (SM Illustrations 9 and 10).
cases: SM Example 12: control of the board obtained on 1 July 20X1 → acquisition date 1 July, not the 1 April 'appointed date', 1 June agreement, 15 July payment or 1 August share transfer.
Court-approved schemes and regulatory approvals: control usually does not pass until substantive approvals are obtained (SM Illustrations 9 and 10).

cards.front: Purchase consideration and acquisition-related costs: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Consideration transferred = acquisition-date fair values of assets transferred (including cash), liabilities incurred to former owners, and equity interests issued (plus contingent consideration). Non-monetary assets transferred are remeasured to fair value with the gain/loss in profit or loss — unless they stay within the combined entity (then carrying amount, no gain). Replacement share-based awards are measured under Ind AS 102. Acquisition-related costs (finder's fees, due diligence, legal, advisory, valuation, bonuses for the deal) are expensed ; costs of issuing debt or equity follow Ind AS 32/109.
back.explanation: Land transferred to former owners: fair value is consideration; land derecognised with gain/loss in profit or loss. SM Illustrations 13–14 test which costs are expensed vs deducted from equity (share issue costs).
cases: SM Illustrations 13–14 test which costs are expensed vs deducted from equity (share issue costs).

cards.front: Memory hook: Consideration and acquisition costs?

back.simplified: Costs of doing the deal → P&L; costs of issuing shares → equity.

cards.front: Business combination achieved in stages (step acquisition): what is the rule?

back.simplified: When control is obtained in stages, the acquirer remeasures its previously held equity interest at acquisition-date fair value and recognises any gain or loss in profit or loss (or OCI if the interest was designated at FVOCI). Amounts previously in OCI are treated as if the interest were disposed of directly. The fair value of the previously held interest is added to consideration in computing goodwill. Before control, the interest is under Ind AS 109 or Ind AS 28.
back.explanation: 15% → 35% → 100% (65% more on 31 March 20X3): acquisition date is when control is obtained, 31 March 20X3. A party to a joint operation obtaining control of it remeasures its previously held interest — a step acquisition.
cases: SM Illustration 11 works the remeasurement and goodwill.

cards.front: Memory hook: Step acquisition?

back.simplified: Step up = sell the old stake at fair value, buy the whole at fair value.

cards.front: Worked example: Step acquisition — what does ICAI's illustration show?

back.simplified: SM Illustration 11 works the remeasurement and goodwill.

cards.front: Combination without transfer of consideration (incl. by contract alone): what is the rule?

back.simplified: The acquisition method applies when control is obtained without consideration: (a) the acquiree buys back enough of its own shares for an investor to obtain control; (b) minority veto rights lapse; (c) combination by contract alone (stapling, dual-listed). By contract alone, the acquiree's net assets are attributed to its owners as NCI — possibly 100%. Goodwill uses the acquisition-date fair value of the acquirer's interest in place of consideration.
back.explanation: SM Illustration 12 (business combination by contract alone).
cases: SM Illustration 12 (business combination by contract alone).

cards.front: Contingent consideration: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Recognise contingent consideration at acquisition-date fair value as part of consideration (increasing goodwill). Classify as liability or equity under Ind AS 32; a right to return of consideration is an asset. Later: changes from new information about facts at the acquisition date within the measurement period adjust goodwill; changes from post-acquisition events (targets met, share price) are not measurement-period adjustments — equity-classified is not remeasured ; other contingent consideration is remeasured at fair value through profit or loss .
back.explanation: SM Example 14: additional ₹20 million cash if targets met, fair value ₹15 million at acquisition → financial liability; if the target becomes less likely, remeasure through P&L, not goodwill. Payments to selling shareholders who stay as employees may be remuneration, not consideration — see employee contingent payments .
cases: SM Example 14: additional ₹20 million cash if targets met, fair value ₹15 million at acquisition → financial liability; if the target becomes less likely, remeasure through P&L, not goodwill.

cards.front: Memory hook: Contingent consideration?

back.simplified: Day 1 fair value into goodwill; later changes → P&L (unless equity or measurement-period facts).

sections.title: Recognising and measuring what is acquired

cards.front: Step 3 — recognising identifiable assets and liabilities: what is the rule?

back.simplified: At the acquisition date recognise, separately from goodwill, the identifiable assets acquired, liabilities assumed and any NCI. They must meet the definitions of assets and liabilities (using the Framework for the Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements , not the 2021 Conceptual Framework) and be part of what was exchanged. Items the acquiree never recognised (internally generated brands, patents, customer relationships) can be recognised. Classify/designate on conditions at the acquisition date (FVTPL/amortised cost/FVOCI, hedges, embedded derivatives) — except a lease where the acquiree is lessor (classified at inception, not reassessed).
back.explanation: Planned restructuring or exit costs the acquirer is not obliged to incur are not liabilities at acquisition — post-combination expenses. Only assets and liabilities that are part of the deal; separate transactions follow other Ind AS.

cards.front: Measurement at fair value and the exceptions: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Measure identifiable assets and liabilities at acquisition-date fair value , with exceptions. Recognition exception : contingent liabilities — recognise a present obligation from past events whose fair value is reliably measurable even if an outflow is not probable (Ind AS 37 tests do not apply). Recognition and measurement exceptions : income taxes (Ind AS 12), employee benefits (Ind AS 19), indemnification assets (same basis as the indemnified item), leases where acquiree is lessee (Ind AS 116 at PV of remaining payments, ROU adjusted for favourable/unfavourable terms; short-term/low-value exempt). Measurement exceptions : reacquired rights (remaining contractual term, no renewals), share-
back.explanation: SM Example 15: suit for ₹10 million disclosed as contingent liability by the acquiree; fair value ₹2 million → recognised in acquisition accounting. SM Example 16: claim ₹250, seller indemnifies losses above ₹100 → liability ₹250, indemnification asset ₹150.
cases: SM Example 15: suit for ₹10 million disclosed as contingent liability by the acquiree; fair value ₹2 million → recognised in acquisition accounting.
SM Example 16: claim ₹250, seller indemnifies losses above ₹100 → liability ₹250, indemnification asset ₹150.

cards.front: Memory hook: Fair value and exceptions?

back.simplified: Exceptions 'TEIL' for recognition+measurement (Tax, Employee benefits, Indemnification, Lessee leases); 'RSHI' measurement only (Reacquired rights, Share-based, Held for sale, Insurance); Contingent liabilities = recognition only.

cards.front: Identifiable intangible assets, assembled workforce: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Recognise an intangible separately from goodwill if it is identifiable: it meets the contractual-legal criterion (even if not separable) or the separability criterion (capable of being sold, licensed, rented or exchanged, alone or with a related contract, asset or liability — evidence of exchange for similar assets suffices). An assembled workforce and potential contracts under negotiation are not identifiable → subsumed in goodwill .
back.explanation: Nuclear plant operating licence (contractual-legal, not separable) — may be combined with the plant if useful lives are similar. Customer lists are usually separable unless confidentiality prohibits exchange (SM Example 17); depositor relationships separable with deposit liabilities; unpatented know-how separable with the trademark.
cases: Customer lists are usually separable unless confidentiality prohibits exchange (SM Example 17); depositor relationships separable with deposit liabilities; unpatented know-how separable with the trademark.

cards.front: Memory hook: Intangibles in a business combination?

back.simplified: Identifiable = Contract/law OR Separable. Workforce → goodwill.

cards.front: Reacquired rights: what is the rule?

back.simplified: A right the acquirer had granted to the acquiree (franchise to use its trade name, technology licence) and now reacquires is an identifiable intangible recognised separately from goodwill, measured on the remaining contractual term without renewals , and amortised over that term. If the contract terms are favourable or unfavourable relative to market, recognise a settlement gain or loss separately from the combination.
back.explanation: If later sold to a third party, include its carrying amount in the gain or loss on sale. SM Illustrations 19–20.
cases: SM Illustrations 19–20.

sections.title: Goodwill, NCI, bargain purchase, measurement period

cards.front: Non-controlling interest at acquisition: what is the rule?

back.simplified: For each business combination, measure NCI that are present ownership interests entitling holders to a proportionate share of net assets on liquidation at either (a) fair value (full goodwill) or (b) their proportionate share of the recognised identifiable net assets (partial goodwill). All other components of NCI at fair value unless another Ind AS requires otherwise.
back.explanation: Fair value per share of NCI may differ from the acquirer's because of a control premium or a discount for lack of control. Choice is made combination by combination. SM Illustration 29.
cases: Choice is made combination by combination. SM Illustration 29.

cards.front: Step 4 — goodwill: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Goodwill = (a) consideration transferred at acquisition-date fair value + (b) NCI measured under Ind AS 103 + (c) in a step acquisition, acquisition-date fair value of the previously held interest; minus (d) net identifiable assets acquired measured under Ind AS 103. Where only equity is exchanged and the acquiree's equity is more reliably measured, use the acquiree's equity fair value; where no consideration is transferred, use the fair value of the acquirer's interest.
back.explanation: Goodwill is not amortised; tested for impairment under Ind AS 36. Reverse acquisition goodwill uses deemed consideration (see reverse acquisitions ).

cards.front: Memory hook: Goodwill computation?

back.simplified: Goodwill = C + NCI + PHI − Net assets.

cards.front: Bargain purchase (capital reserve): what is the rule?

back.simplified: If net assets exceed consideration + NCI + previously held interest, first reassess identification and measurement of all assets, liabilities, NCI, previously held interest and consideration. If a gain remains and there is clear evidence of the reason (e.g. forced sale), recognise it in OCI and accumulate it in equity as capital reserve ; if there is no clear evidence, recognise it directly in equity as capital reserve . The gain is attributed to the acquirer, not NCI.
back.explanation: Indian carve-out from IFRS 3 (which takes the gain to profit or loss). SM Example 18: assets sold under a competition authority's deadline — likely bargain purchase. SM Illustration 21.
cases: SM Example 18: assets sold under a competition authority's deadline — likely bargain purchase. SM Illustration 21.

cards.front: Memory hook: Bargain purchase gain?

back.simplified: Bargain gain: clear reason → OCI → capital reserve; no clear reason → straight to capital reserve. Never P&L.

cards.front: Measurement period (provisional accounting): what is the rule?

back.simplified: If initial accounting is incomplete, report provisional amounts. During the measurement period , adjust them retrospectively (against goodwill) for new information about facts and circumstances that existed at the acquisition date , and recognise additional assets or liabilities. The period ends when the information is obtained or is not obtainable, and cannot exceed one year from the acquisition date. After that, corrections are errors under Ind AS 8; changes from post-acquisition events are not measurement-period adjustments.
back.explanation: SM Illustrations 22–23 work provisional values revised within and after the period.
cases: SM Illustrations 22–23 work provisional values revised within and after the period.

cards.front: Memory hook: Measurement period (max 1 year)?

back.simplified: Existed at day 1 + found within 1 year → adjust goodwill; otherwise P&L or Ind AS 8 error.

sections.title: What is part of the combination

cards.front: What is part of the business combination; pre-existing relationships: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Account only for what was exchanged for the acquiree. Separate transactions include: settling a pre-existing relationship between acquirer and acquiree; remunerating employees or former owners for future services ; reimbursing the acquiree or its owners for the acquirer's acquisition costs. Factors: reasons for the transaction, who initiated it, and its timing. A pre-existing relationship is settled at the lesser of (a) the favourable/unfavourable amount relative to market and (b) any stated settlement provision; non-contractual (e.g. lawsuit) at fair value — the gain or loss to profit or loss , not goodwill.
back.explanation: Reacquired rights in a pre-existing franchise are capitalised and amortised (see reacquired rights ). SM Illustration 24.
cases: SM Illustration 24.

cards.front: Memory hook: Separate transactions and pre-existing relationships?

back.simplified: Ask Why, Who, When — benefit to acquirer = separate transaction.

cards.front: Contingent payments to employees or selling shareholders: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Indicators of whether payments are consideration or post-combination remuneration : (a) continuing employment — payments automatically forfeited if employment ends are remuneration ; (b) duration of required employment vs payment period; (c) level of other remuneration; (d) incremental payments to employee-sellers vs non-employee sellers; (e) number of shares held by those who stay; (f) linkage to valuation (low end of a range → consideration); (g) formula — multiple of earnings suggests consideration, a percentage of earnings suggests profit sharing; (h) other agreements (below-market leases, non-competes).
back.explanation: SM Illustrations 25–26 (payments to former owners who stay as employees).
cases: SM Illustrations 25–26 (payments to former owners who stay as employees).

cards.front: Memory hook: Contingent payments to employee-sellers?

back.simplified: Leave the job, lose the money → salary, not price.

cards.front: Replacement and non-replacement share-based awards: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Replacement awards : the portion attributable to pre-combination service = market-based measure of the acquiree award × vesting period completed ÷ greater of total vesting period and original vesting period → part of consideration ; the rest (and any excess of the replacement over the acquiree award) → post-combination remuneration . If the acquirer replaces awards it was not obliged to replace (awards would expire), the whole measure is remuneration. Non-replacement awards : vested → NCI at market-based measure; unvested → pre-combination portion to NCI, the rest employee cost over remaining vesting (credited to NCI).
back.explanation: SM Example 19: pre-combination portion ₹100, 95% expected to vest → ₹95 in consideration; later changes in expected vesting go to remuneration cost. SM Illustration 28: award ₹500, 2 of 5 years served → ₹200 to NCI; ₹300 expensed over the reduced 2-year remaining period.
cases: SM Example 19: pre-combination portion ₹100, 95% expected to vest → ₹95 in consideration; later changes in expected vesting go to remuneration cost.
SM Illustration 28: award ₹500, 2 of 5 years served → ₹200 to NCI; ₹300 expensed over the reduced 2-year remaining period.

cards.front: Memory hook: Share-based awards in a combination?

back.simplified: Pre-combination share = measure × served ÷ max(total, original).

cards.front: Subsequent measurement of items from the combination: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Generally other Ind AS apply after acquisition, except: reacquired rights — amortise over the remaining contractual period; contingent liabilities — higher of the Ind AS 37 amount and the initial amount less cumulative Ind AS 115 income; indemnification assets — same basis as the indemnified item, subject to contractual limits and collectability, derecognised only when collected, sold or the right is lost; contingent consideration — equity not remeasured; others at fair value through profit or loss.

cards.front: Disclosures: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Disclose for each combination in the period (or after the reporting date before approval): name and description of acquiree, acquisition date, % voting interests, reasons and how control was obtained, qualitative factors making up goodwill, fair value of consideration by class, contingent consideration and indemnification assets (amount, basis, range), acquired receivables, amounts for each major class of assets/liabilities, contingent liabilities, goodwill deductible for tax, separate transactions and acquisition-related costs, bargain purchase gain (OCI/equity and reasons), NCI and its measurement basis, step-acquisition fair value and gain, and acquiree revenue and profit since acquisitio

cards.front: Common control business combinations — scope: what is the rule?

back.simplified: A common control business combination involves entities or businesses ultimately controlled by the same party or parties both before and after the combination, where that control is not transitory . NCI levels are irrelevant. The controlling party may be an individual or a group of individuals acting together under a contractual arrangement, who need not prepare Ind AS statements.
back.explanation: Examples: merger of fellow subsidiaries, merger of a subsidiary into its parent, acquisition of an entity from within the group, bringing entities under common control into a legal structure. Transitory control (structured to fall in Appendix C briefly before a real change of control) → Ind AS 103 acquisition method; a combination before an IPO is not transitory merely for that reason.
cases: SM Illustrations 30–33.

cards.front: Pooling of interests method: what is the rule?

back.simplified: Account for common control combinations by the pooling of interests method : (i) assets and liabilities at carrying amounts ; (ii) no fair value adjustments or new assets/liabilities — only harmonise accounting policies ; (iii) restate prior periods as if the combination occurred from the beginning of the earliest period presented (or from the date common control began, if later). Consideration: securities at nominal value ; non-cash assets at fair value. Transferor's retained earnings are aggregated with the transferee's (or transferred to general reserve); identity of reserves is preserved. The difference between (share capital issued + other consideration) and the transferor's share capit
back.explanation: SM Illustrations 34–40 work the journal entries and balance sheets.
cases: SM Illustrations 34–40 work the journal entries and balance sheets.

cards.front: Memory hook: Pooling of interests?

back.simplified: Pooling = Carrying amounts, Restate comparatives, Reserves keep their names, Difference to capital reserve.

practice.prompt:
RST Ltd. prepares consolidated financial statements as at 31st March each year. On 1st July, 2021, RST Ltd. acquired 75% of the equity shares of DHF Ltd. and gained control of DHF Ltd. The issued shares of DHF Ltd. are 1,20,00,000 equity shares. Details of the purchase consideration are as follows:
 On 1st July 2021, RST Ltd. issued two shares for every three shares acquired in DHF Ltd. On 1st July 2021, the market value of an equity share in RST Ltd. was ₹ 6.50 and the market value of an equity share in DHF Ltd. was ₹ 5.50.
 On 30th June 2022, RST Ltd. will make cash payment of ₹ 71,50,000 to the former shareholders of DHF Ltd. who sold their shares to RST Ltd. on 1st July 2021. On 1st July, 2021, RST Ltd. would have to pay interest at an annual rate of 10% on borrowings.
 On 30th June 2023, RST Ltd. may make a cash payment of ₹ 3,00,00,000 to the former shareholders of DHF Ltd. who sold their shares to RST Ltd. on 1st July 2021. This payment is contingent upon the revenues of RST Ltd. growing by 15% over the two-year period from 1st July, 2021 to 30th June, 2023. On 1st July 2021, the fair value of this contingent consideration was ₹ 2,50,00,000. On 31st March 2022, the fair value of the contingent consideration was ₹ 2,20,00,000.
 On 1st July 2021, the carrying values of the identifiable net assets of DHF Ltd. in the books of that company was ₹ 6,00,00,000. On 1st July 2021, the fair values of these net assets was ₹ 7,00,00,000. The rate of deferred tax to apply to temporary differences is 20%.
 During the nine months ended on 31st March 2022, DHF Ltd. had a poorer than expected operating performance. Therefore, on 31st March, 2022 it was necessary for RST Ltd. to recognize an impairment of the goodwill arising on acquisition of DHF Ltd. amounting to 12.50% of its total computed value.
 Compute the impairment of goodwill in the consolidated financial statements of RST Ltd. under the methods permitted by Ind AS 103 for the initial computation of the non-controlling interest in DHF Ltd. at the acquisition date. (5 Marks)

A Limited and B Limited are engaged in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals. On 1st June, 2024, A Limited acquired 15% of equity shares of B Limited. On 1st October, 2024, A Limited obtains control of B Limited when it acquires a further 55% of B Limited's shares, thereby resulting into a total holding of 70%. The fair value of the shares of B Limited was ₹ 40 per share as on that date.
 Prior to the acquisition of additional 55% stake by A Limited on 1st October, 2024, the Balance Sheets of the two companies stood as under: (₹ in lakhs)
  Particulars A Ltd. B Ltd.   Assets     Non-Current Assets    Property, Plant and Equipment 600 400  Investments (6,00,000 Shares of B Ltd. acquired on 1st June, 2024) 210 -  Current Assets    Inventories 500 150  Financial Assets - Trade receivables 450 300  Cash and cash equivalents 400 100  Other Current Assets 200 230  Non-current assets held for sale - 250  Total 2,360 1,430   Equity and Liabilities     Equity: Share Capital – Equity Shares of ₹ 100 each 500 -  Share Capital – Equity Shares of ₹ 10 each - 400  Other Equity 810 225  Non-Current Liabilities - Financial Liabilities: Long-term Borrowings 250 200  Long-term Provisions 50 70  Deferred Tax Liability 40 -  Current Liabilities - Financial Liabilities: Short-term Borrowings 400 285  Trade Payables 310 250  Total 2,360 1,430  In consideration of the additional stake acquired by A Limited on 1st October, 2024, it agreed to pay to each selling shareholder of B Limited a sum of ₹ 15 per share in cash and issue 1 Equity Share of ₹ 100 each of A Limited in lieu of 8 Equity Shares of ₹ 10 each held by the selling shareholder in B Limited. The fair value of the shares of A Limited as on 1st October, 2024 is ₹ 160 per share.
 In addition to the above:
 (a) A Limited agreed to pay an additional payment as consideration that is higher of ₹ 35 lakhs and 25% of any excess profit in the first year, after acquisition over its profits in the preceding one year made by B Limited. This additional amount would be due after 2 years. B Limited has earned ₹ 10 lakhs profit in the preceding year and expects to earn another ₹ 20 lakhs.
 (b) A Limited also agreed to pay one of the promoter shareholders of B Limited a payment of ₹ 15 lakhs provided he stays with the company for two years after acquisition.
 (c) A Limited* had a certain equity settled share-based payment award (Original award) which was replaced by the new award issued by B Limited**. As per the original terms, the vesting period was 4 years and as of the acquisition date, the employees of B Limited have already served 2 years of service. As per the replaced award, the vesting period is reduced to one year (one year from the acquisition date). The fair value of the award on the acquisition date was as under:
 (i) Original Award: ₹ 5 lakhs
 (ii) Replacement Award: ₹ 8 lakhs
 [* PS: Read 'A Limited' as 'B Limited'. ** PS: Read 'B Limited' as 'A Limited'. (ICAI's printed corrections.)]
 (d) The fair value exercise resulted in the following:
 (i) The fair value of Property, Plant and Equipment and Inventory of B Limited as on 1st October, 2024 was ₹ 480 lakhs and ₹ 170 lakhs respectively.
 (ii) The carrying value of Non-Current Asset held for sale of ₹ 250 lakhs of B Limited represents its fair value less cost to sell in accordance with the relevant Ind AS.
 (iii) B Limited has developed and patented a new drug for Parkinson disease which has been approved for clinical use. The cost of developing the drug was ₹ 140 lakhs. Based on early assessment of its sales success, the valuer has estimated its market value at ₹ 200 lakhs.
 (iv) B Limited had a lawsuit for infringement of Trademark pending with a competitor who had made a claim of ₹ 50 lakhs. B Limited has disclosed the same as a contingent liability as it is not probable that the amount would be payable. Management reliably estimated the fair value of the liability to be 10 lakhs. Any sum which would be paid in respect of the lawsuit would be tax deductible.
 (e) The cost of capital of A Limited is 10%. The appropriate discount factor for ₹ 1 @ 10% payable at the end of 1st year is 0.91 and 2nd year is 0.83.
 (f) The applicable tax rate for both the entities is 30%.
 Unless stated otherwise, all items have a fair value and tax base equal to their carrying amounts at the acquisition date. A Limited chooses to measure the Non-Controlling Interest in B Limited as per Proportionate Share of identifiable net assets method.
 You are required to prepare the opening Consolidated Balance Sheet of A Limited as on 1st October, 2024 as per the applicable Ind AS. Working Notes should form part of your answer. (14 Marks)
